title: Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss: Urgent Assessment and Steroid Therapy

evidenceAudit.scope: Adult sudden sensorineural hearing loss: separate conductive from sensorineural loss, avoid routine CT and laboratory tests, audiometry within 14 days, MRI or auditory brainstem response, steroid timing and salvage therapy, from the AAO-HNSF 2019 guideline.
findings: Every dose, threshold and timing was checked against the cited source section on 2026-10-18.
Normal values are typical adult reference ranges; laboratories differ.
unverifiedSections: The opened guideline text names the steroids tested (prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone, dexamethasone) but does not give a dose, duration, taper or intratympanic concentration; the regimen must come from the treating ENT service.
KAS 10 supporting text and the hyperbaric oxygen discussion were not read in full.
SFDA registration of corticosteroids was not verified.
Source pages were read through automated page extraction rather than page-by-page in the original documents, so each figure should be spot-checked against the source during clinical review.

pathophysiology.summary: Sudden sensorineural hearing loss is a sensorineural loss of 30 dB or more over at least 3 consecutive frequencies within 72 hours. Conductive loss must be distinguished first. Retrocochlear pathology can present as sudden loss, so MRI (most sensitive) or auditory brainstem response is used to look for it. Bilateral loss, recurrent episodes and focal neurological findings are modifying factors that change the work-up. Corticosteroids are an option within 2 weeks of onset; therapy after 2 weeks is salvage.

clinicalManagement.title: Distinguish sensorineural from conductive
actions: Establish whether the loss is sensorineural or conductive.
Look for bilateral loss, recurrent episodes and focal neurological findings.

clinicalManagement.title: Order the right tests only
clinicalManagement.timeframe: As soon as possible, within 14 days
actions: Do not order routine head CT or routine laboratory tests.
Obtain audiometry within 14 days of onset.
Evaluate for retrocochlear pathology with MRI (most sensitive) or auditory brainstem response.

clinicalManagement.title: Counsel
actions: Explain the natural history, benefits and risks of treatment and the limits of the evidence.

clinicalManagement.title: Steroid therapy
actions: Offer corticosteroids as initial therapy within 2 weeks of onset; the regimen is chosen by the ENT service because the guideline text opened gives no dose.
Hyperbaric oxygen with steroids is an option within 2 weeks, or as salvage within 1 month.

clinicalManagement.title: Salvage and follow-up
actions: If recovery is incomplete 2 to 6 weeks after onset, offer or refer for intratympanic steroids.
Do not routinely prescribe antivirals, thrombolytics, vasodilators or vasoactive substances.
Follow-up audiometry at the end of treatment and within 6 months; counsel about audiologic rehabilitation for residual loss or tinnitus.

medicationPlan.note: The AAO-HNSF text opened lists prednisone, prednisolone, methylprednisolone and dexamethasone as systemic steroids and notes a 10- to 14-day course has minimal Cushing-like effect, but gives no dose, taper or intratympanic concentration. The treating ENT service sets the regimen. SFDA registration was not verified; check hospital formulary.

diagnosticCriteria.threshold: 30 dB or more loss at 3 or more consecutive frequencies within 72 hours.
As soon as possible and within 14 days of onset (KAS 4).
Offer within 2 weeks of onset (KAS 8, option).
Incomplete recovery 2 to 6 weeks after onset (KAS 10).
